import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 38

*Reference:*
- [erdosproblems.com/38](https://www.erdosproblems.com/38)
- [Er56](Erdős, P., Problems and results in additive number theory.
  Colloque sur la Théorie des Nombres, Bruxelles, 1955 (1956), 127-137.)
-/

open Set Pointwise

namespace Erdos38

open scoped Classical in
/--
Does there exist $B \subset \mathbb{N}$ which is not an additive basis,
but is such that for every set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ of Schnirelmann density $\alpha$
and every $N$ there exists $b \in B$ such that
$$
  \lvert (A \cup (A+b)) \cap \{1, \ldots, N\} \rvert \geq (\alpha + f(\alpha)) N
$$
where $f(\alpha) > 0$ for $0 < \alpha < 1$?

Note: here Erdős seems to use a slightly weaker notion of an additive basis (see [Er56] at the top
of page 135). In particular, for this problem, a set is an additive basis of order $k$ if every
natural number can be written as a sum of _at most_ $k$ elements of the set, rather than as a sum of
_precisely_ $k$ elements.

A positive [solution](https://github.com/spicylemonade/erdos-38) was given by GPT 5.5 Pro
(prompted by gebyjaff, cleanup by Liam Price); in fact a sparse random set $B$ has this property,
with $f(\alpha)\gg \alpha (1-\alpha)^2$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
"https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/38#post-6131"]
theorem erdos_38 : answer(True) ↔
    ∃ B : Set ℕ, ¬ B.IsWeakAddBasis ∧ ∃ f : ℝ → ℝ, (∀ α, 0 < α → α < 1 → f α > 0) ∧
      ∀ (A : Set ℕ) (N : ℕ),
        let α := schnirelmannDensity A
        ∃ b ∈ B, (Ioc 0 N ∩ (A ∪ (A + {b}))).ncard ≥ (α + f α) * N := by
  sorry

end Erdos38

reformulations.difference: The density-increment clause includes N = 0 and densities α = 0 or 1, whereas Theorem 1 of the cited solution restricts this clause to N ≥ 1 and 0 < α < 1.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The restricted clause already forces B to be nonempty: apply it to the positive odd integers, whose Schnirelmann density is 1/2. Extend its function f by zero outside (0,1). At the endpoint densities, A alone satisfies |A ∩ {1,…,N}| ≥ αN, so any member of B works. At N = 0 the inequality is 0 ≥ 0. Conversely, the unrestricted clause immediately implies the restricted one. The equivalence for the exact existential RHS was proved in /workspace/review/scratch.lean as Review38.problem_rhs_iff_interior, without sorry or additional axioms.

reformulations.difference: The theorem uses IsWeakAddBasis, with a variable number of summands bounded by one uniform order, rather than an exact-order additive-basis predicate.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: This is precisely Erdős’s convention here: Er56, p. 135, defines a basis of order k by saying that every integer is the sum of 'k or fewer b-s'. The Lean predicate unfolds to ∃ k, ∀ n, ∃ m ≤ k, n ∈ m • B. I proved its equivalence to the corresponding Fin m-indexed sum representation. Repetition is allowed, and zero is represented by the empty sum, so using ℕ introduces no extra restriction.

review.notes: The sole theorem faithfully states the problem. The current source records an affirmative, Lean-verified solution, agreeing with research solved, answer(True), and the proof citation. All counted sets are finite, so ncard's infinite-set default is unreachable. Boundary tests also establish that the increment property forces 1 ∈ B. The cited external proof contains no sorry or custom axioms, but targets Mathlib v4.28.0 and did not compile unchanged under the supplied v4.33.1 environment; independent kernel verification of that certificate is therefore not claimed. Its explicit sparsity certificates supply the required non-weak-basis conclusion: adjoining zero preserves sparsity, while a weak basis becomes an exact-order basis after adjoining zero. This addresses the external proof's use of an asymptotic exact-order basis definition.
